<reason>B built the cleaner path to victory by structurally dividing the motion: the fee half was shown largely redundant with existing drip-pricing law and platform practice (a point A's "compliance need not change" concession fed directly), and the house-rule half — the motion's only genuinely new content — was attacked with a plausible defensive-inflation mechanism (legal duty converts omission from commercial risk to violation, producing privacy-policy-style bloat). B also answered A's best concrete harm (late-arriving family) with a real mechanism: hosts hiding disqualifying rules gain cancellations, not bookings, so the mandate's unique reach is the rare irrational host while costs fall on everyone. A landed genuine hits — Q1 forced B to abandon its original contract-enforceability mechanism, and A corrected B's "two mandated touchpoints" mischaracterization — but A leaned increasingly on a single example, underdeveloped its strongest remaining ground (non-universal coverage of existing law), and never escaped B's "sliver" framing. Both sides were epistemically disciplined, format-compliant, and did real weighing; B simply made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: answered A's Q1 by cleanly pivoting from the vulnerable enforceability mechanism to a regulated-display penalty mechanism, then defused A's "routine vs. disruptive" inconsistency charge in two sentences by assigning redundancy to the fee half and disruption to the rule half — resolving the debate's central clash while keeping the weighing frame intact.</best_rebuttal>
